questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The planographic principle of lithography
questions.learningObjective: Explain how grease repels ink on a damp stone.
questions.stem: Pinned beside the depot route map, a print-room notice asks why a greasy crayon drawing on a damp limestone slab prints cleanly.

options.text: The grease makes the marked stone reject the oily printing ink
The crayon line is cut into the slab, so ink is held in the groove
options.misconception: confuses planographic printing with intaglio engraving

options.text: The whole slab is inked, then the bare stone is scraped away
options.misconception: imagines a relief block instead of a flat stone

options.text: The image prints only where the stone is dampened with clean water
options.misconception: believes damp areas take the ink rather than rejecting it

questions.explanation: Lithography is planographic: image and blank share one flat plane. Grease in the crayon repels oily ink, and damp stone attracts it, so only the drawn mark prints. Grooves and scraping describe relief or intaglio.
questions.hint: Ask where the ink ends up staying.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The layer logic of screen printing
questions.learningObjective: Read a set of coverage figures as separate colour layers.
questions.stem: On the transit planner's board, a graphic standards sheet lists three screens with ink coverage of 60, 40 and 25 percent respectively.

options.text: Three passes of a single colour printed to deepen the same flat tone
options.misconception: reads multiple screens as repeated passes of one ink

options.text: Three separate colours printed one over another to build the final image
One screen printed in three densities to simulate shading on one plate
options.misconception: thinks screens vary density rather than colour

options.text: A single screen divided into three stencil densities for one hue
options.misconception: confuses mesh counts with printed colour layers

questions.explanation: Screen printing separates an image into colour layers; each screen prints one ink through its open mesh, and the layers combine into the picture. Repeated passes of one ink merely deepen a single flat tone.
questions.hint: Count the inks, not the pulls.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal inversion on a photographic negative
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a photographic negative reverses the tones of the scene.
questions.stem: A memo filed on the planner's board notes that a photographic negative shows a bright sun as a dark disc and asks why prints look normal.

answer.exemplar: A photographic negative records brightness as density: the brightest parts of the scene expose the film most and so appear darkest on the negative, while shadowed areas are barely exposed and remain clear. When light is passed through the negative onto sensitised paper, the dense areas block the light and print as light, while the clear areas expose the paper and print dark. The result is a normal-toned image with the inversion occurring in the negative alone.

questions.explanation: A negative stores the scene in reversed tone: bright subjects sit in dense areas, dark subjects in thin ones. Printing through it restores normal appearance. A left-right mirror flip is a different fault.
questions.hint: Think about what passes through.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirrored surface of a daguerreotype
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a daguerreotype plate covered by a mirrored inscription.
questions.stem: A depot display note measures a daguerreotype plate 8.0 centimetres wide; its mirrored inscription occupies 4.0 centimetres. What percentage of the plate width does the inscription cover?
questions.explanation: The mirrored inscription spans 4.0 of the 8.0 centimetre plate, so its share is 4.0 divided by 8.0, which is 0.5, or 50 percent. Half the plate width carries the reversed lettering, leaving equal margins at the two ends.
questions.hint: Divide the inscription length by the plate width.

questions.topic: What the wet-plate tintype buys
questions.learningObjective: Identify the direct-positive character of a wet-plate tintype.

stimulus.body: The depot print-room bulletin for Tuesday reads: collodion is poured on the glass, sensitised, exposed wet in the camera, and developed on the spot. Plates are one-offs.

questions.stem: Using the Tuesday bulletin, a transit planner decides which claim about the wet-plate tintype is correct.

options.text: It records the scene only as a shadow, so it cannot hold a tonal range
options.misconception: believes one-of-a-kind plates cannot carry tone

options.text: It makes a reusable negative that can be printed as many copies as needed
options.misconception: confuses a direct positive with a reusable negative

options.text: It produces a direct positive, so the plate itself shows the scene as it will appear
It fixes the image on the plate during printing, so exposure does not matter
options.misconception: thinks the image is printed rather than exposed

questions.explanation: A wet-plate tintype is a direct positive: the exposed, developed plate itself is the finished image. No negative is made, and the process is quick because the plate must stay wet. The other options describe a negative workflow or a print.
questions.hint: Does the plate or a negative hold the image?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal range in a gelatin silver print
questions.learningObjective: Connect the density of a gelatin silver print to exposure and development.
questions.stem: A transit planner's board carries a two-part test: first, what does density in a gelatin silver print represent; second, how is that density produced.

options.text: First, the grain size of the paper; second, by choosing a coarse fibre stock
options.misconception: confuses paper grain with the scale of the image

options.text: First, the size of the image on the paper; second, by enlarging the negative during printing
options.misconception: thinks density comes from enlarging the picture rather than exposure

options.text: First, the colour of the highlights; second, by tinting the print in a sepia bath
options.misconception: assumes tone in a black and white print comes from colouring

options.text: First, the amount of black silver deposited; second, by exposing the paper so more silver forms

questions.explanation: Density in a gelatin silver print is the quantity of black metallic silver deposited on the paper, controlled by exposure and development. A larger image, a tint bath or coarse grain would change size or colour, not the tonal scale.
questions.hint: Ask what a black area actually contains.

questions.topic: Three-colour construction of a colour print
questions.learningObjective: Describe how three subtractive separations build a colour print.
questions.stem: In a depot bulletin about colour printing, a poster's yellow, magenta and cyan separations are described before the sheets are run.

options.text: Each separation is a full colour photograph that is stacked for extra depth
options.misconception: thinks separations are complete colour images stacked together

options.text: Each separation records where one subtractive ink is laid, and the layers build the colours
Each separation is printed in black to build the shadows between colour plates
options.misconception: believes all separations are printed in black ink

options.text: Each separation holds a random colour that is rotated until the print looks right
options.misconception: imagines colour plates are chosen at random during printing

questions.explanation: Three-colour printing is subtractive: yellow, magenta and cyan inks are each recorded as a separation, and their overlapping densities subtract light to give a wide range of hues. Stacking colour images or printing everything in black cannot do that.
questions.hint: Subtractive colour removes light.

questions.learningObjective: Compare a greasy crayon drawing with a scratched stone.
questions.stem: A calibration sheet on the planner's board compares two stone proofs: one drawn entirely with greasy crayon, the other scratched with a needle.

options.text: Both proofs print equally, because every stone is inked to the same overall density
options.misconception: believes ink coverage ignores the drawn image

options.text: The scratched proof prints darker, because scratches cut deep valleys that hold more ink
options.misconception: assumes scratching works like an engraved plate

options.text: The crayon proof prints darker, because grease on the stone repels ink where the image is drawn
The crayon proof prints lighter, because grease absorbs the ink into the stone surface
options.misconception: reverses the effect of grease and damp stone

questions.explanation: Greasy crayon marks the image so ink is repelled there and the drawing prints solid. Scratching a stone opens ink-holding pits, which is intaglio logic; in lithography the ink lies flat on the surface.
questions.hint: Compare a grease mark with a cut groove.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The layer logic of screen printing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why screen printing needs a separate mesh for each colour.
questions.stem: A training note on the transit planner's board asks why a screen-printed poster needs a separate mesh for each colour rather than one mesh inked repeatedly.

answer.exemplar: Each screen carries a stencil of the areas that will receive one particular ink, so the mesh itself defines where that colour appears. Printing the same mesh repeatedly in different inks would deposit every ink in the same places, producing muddy overlaps instead of separate colour areas. A separate stencil per colour lets each ink be confined to its own part of the design and combined optically where the layers overlap, which is what gives clean, flat areas of colour.

questions.explanation: The stencil in each screen defines where its ink may land, so one mesh per colour keeps each ink in its own zone and lets overlaps mix properly. One mesh printed in several inks would put every colour in the same places.
questions.hint: Each stencil controls one ink only.

questions.stem: A darkroom notice records a negative in which the brightest scene area reaches 2.8 density while the darkest reaches only 0.1. What is the density range of that negative?
questions.explanation: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest readings: 2.8 minus 0.1 equals 2.7. A larger range means the negative separates shadow from highlight more strongly when printed.
questions.hint: Subtract the lowest reading from the highest.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the stage that produces a laterally reversed daguerreotype.

stimulus.body: The archive display note for the daguerreotype reads: visitors holding the case at arm's length see the doorway sign written from right to left. The plate shows no trace of retouching or hand colouring.

options.text: The engraving of the plate, which cuts the lettering in reverse to save time
options.misconception: assumes the plate was engraved rather than exposed

options.text: The polishing of the silvered plate, which reverses the grain of the metal
options.misconception: blames the polishing stage for a lens effect

options.text: The mercury vapour, which settles on the image and mirrors it during development
options.misconception: believes the developer mirrors the image

options.text: The camera lens, which forms an inverted image that is never flipped back

questions.explanation: A lens forms an inverted and reversed image of the scene, and the daguerreotype plate keeps that orientation. The polished silver surface is simply the light-sensitive record; nothing in the making reverses it again.
questions.hint: The image is fixed by the lens, not later.

questions.topic: What the wet-plate tintype buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wet plate must stay moist and what that gains.
questions.stem: The planner's board carries a two-part question: first, why must the collodion plate stay moist; second, what practical gain does the wet plate bring to a busy studio.

options.text: First, the plate must stay moist so mercury cannot settle; second, the portrait is printed in seconds
options.misconception: thinks mercury develops the image and the plate prints it

options.text: First, the silver salts must remain active; second, the image can be developed at once
First, moisture keeps the glass from warping; second, one plate can serve many sitters
options.misconception: believes wet plates are reusable and warp only when dry

options.text: First, the wet plate reflects more light into the lens; second, the picture appears sharper
options.misconception: confuses plate moisture with focus and sharpness

questions.explanation: Silver salts lose sensitivity once the collodion dries, so a wet plate must be exposed and developed without drying. That immediacy is the practical gain: a portrait is finished in minutes rather than sent off for processing.
questions.hint: Collodion keeps the salts sensitive.

questions.topic: Tonal range in a gelatin silver print
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that paper grade alone sets the tonal range.
questions.stem: A notice at the depot claims a print's tonal range depends only on the grade of paper used, and asks the planner to judge the claim.

options.text: Correct, because a softer grade always yields the widest range of greys
options.misconception: assumes softer paper always means more tonal range

options.text: Correct, because paper grade alone fixes how much black the print can reach
options.misconception: believes paper grade alone sets the tonal range

options.text: Incorrect, because tone also depends on exposure, development and the negative's own density
Incorrect, only because the printing paper must be glossy to hold a full range
options.misconception: links tonal range to surface gloss rather than exposure

questions.explanation: Paper grade sets the contrast the emulsion will give, but exposure, development time and the negative's own density also decide how the range of greys appears. Gloss has nothing to do with it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The planographic principle of lithography
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a lithographic stone must be kept damp during inking.
questions.stem: A drafting note on the transit planner's board asks why a lithographic stone must be kept damp while ink is being rolled onto it.

answer.exemplar: The ink is a heavy, oily substance that will not adhere to a clean, dry limestone, so the stone is kept damp to make the blank areas take the ink. The dampness also prevents the grease drawn into the image from being displaced. Where the artist has drawn with greasy crayon, the grease repels the ink and the image remains clean; everywhere else the damp surface takes the ink and prints solid. Drying the stone would let the ink sit everywhere and fill the image.

questions.explanation: Oily ink will not stick to clean dry stone, so dampness makes the blank areas take the ink while the greasy drawn lines repel it. Drying the surface would let ink settle everywhere and fill in the image.
questions.hint: Damp stone takes ink; greasy lines do not.

options.text: A photographic positive, because the dark hair has come out light
options.misconception: confuses a light hair area with a correctly rendered positive

A drawing on film, because the tones were brushed on by hand

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Three-colour construction of a colour print
questions.learningObjective: Explain why colour printing works by subtracting light.
questions.stem: A planner's board note asks why three-colour printing uses subtractive inks rather than printing light directly onto the paper.

answer.exemplar: Paper reflects light, so a print cannot add brightness to a page; it can only subtract wavelengths from what is reflected. Subtractive inks such as yellow, magenta and cyan absorb the bands of light they represent, and their overlapping densities build a wide range of colours from the same reflected white. Printing with coloured light instead would need light sources rather than inks, and the result would depend on the viewing room rather than on the sheet itself.

questions.explanation: Paper only reflects light, so inks work by absorbing parts of it. Yellow, magenta and cyan dyes absorb their bands and overlap to build other hues, and the range comes from the sheet's densities, not added light.
questions.hint: Paper reflects; it cannot emit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal range in a gelatin silver print
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fine silver grains allow a continuous range of greys.
questions.stem: A printing note on the planner's board asks why a gelatin silver print can hold a continuous range of greys rather than a few flat tones.

answer.exemplar: The print's silver is deposited as many microscopic particles rather than as a single solid grain of ink. Each tiny particle reduces the light reflected from the paper by a small amount, and the eye reads the summed effect of millions of them as a smooth tone. Because the amount of silver varies smoothly with exposure, the paper can carry an almost unlimited number of distinct greys between paper white and silver black, which is why a continuous tonal range is possible at all.

questions.explanation: Silver forms as countless separate particles, each cutting reflected light a little, so small exposure changes give small continuous tone changes. That grain-by-grain behaviour allows an unlimited number of greys between white and black.
questions.hint: Tone comes from many tiny grains.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature that makes a process planographic.

questions.stem: Using the notice, a transit planner identifies which single feature makes this a planographic process.

options.text: The stone is replaced by a metal sheet that carries the recessed marks
options.misconception: confuses the stone with a metal plate

options.text: The drawing is scratched into the stone with a needle before any ink is applied
options.misconception: reads a scraped step into intaglio work

options.text: The image is inked by rolling over raised areas that stand above the blank
options.misconception: mistakes the planographic process for relief printing

options.text: The image and the blank share the same level, with no parts cut below the surface

questions.explanation: Planographic printing keeps the image and blank on one level; nothing is cut away or left standing. Rolling ink across the flat surface covers the blank and is repelled by the greasy image, the reverse of working in recesses.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the wet-plate tintype buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fast wet plate still records a full tonal range.
questions.stem: A production note on the planner's board asks why a wet-plate tintype, made in minutes, still records a full range of tonal values.

answer.exemplar: Tone on a tintype depends on how much light reaches each part of the plate, and the wet collodion with silver salts is sensitive enough to record very small differences in that light. As the plate is exposed, silver deposits form in proportion to the light falling on it, so a shaded cheek receives fewer and smaller silver particles than a lit forehead. The image therefore carries the same continuous tonal information that a paper print shows, even though the medium and the speed are so different.

questions.explanation: The wet collodion with silver salts registers small differences in light, and silver deposits in proportion to the light received, so shadows and highlights separate as tone. Working quickly does not reduce that tonal range.
questions.hint: Tone follows the light that falls on the plate.

options.misconception: claims three inks cannot produce a wide range of hues

questions.explanation: Each colour comes from its own plate, so any failure to align the three shifts colours at every edge and border of the image. Exposure and the number of separations matter, but neither can rescue a registration error.

A single negative exposed three times, so densities have added together

options.text: Three scenes of different brightness, recorded on one sheet of film
options.misconception: believes the window changed between the three shots

questions.explanation: In all three negatives the window is the brightest part, and it reads darkest where exposure was longest, since more light made the film denser. The scene never changed, so the sequence documents exposure.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirrored surface of a daguerreotype
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the artistic significance of the daguerreotype's reversed image.
questions.stem: A guide note on the board asks why daguerreotypes are valued as the earliest photographs when the plate image is reversed and fragile.

answer.exemplar: The daguerreotype is valuable because it was the first process to fix a real image from a lens onto a surface that could be kept, and it did so with an exposure measured in minutes rather than hours. Its reversed orientation is a limitation of the optics, since a lens projects an inverted image and the plate was never flipped, but the process still produced true tonal records of faces and places. Its fragility has led to protective cases and to countless rephotographs, yet the original plates remain a distinct and irreplaceable achievement.

questions.explanation: Its importance lies in being the first process to fix a lens-formed image on a keepable surface with a short exposure. The reversed orientation is a limitation of the optics, not a failure of the process.
questions.hint: Judge the process, not the orientation.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal inversion on a photographic negative
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one negative can yield prints of different brightness.
questions.stem: A drafting sheet on the planner's board asks why a photographer can print several different brightnesses from one negative without changing the negative itself.

answer.exemplar: Exposure time and the contrast of the printing paper, not the negative, decide how the image appears on the sheet. Making the exposure longer lets more light pass through the negative's dense areas, so the print comes out darker, while a shorter exposure gives a paler result. By changing either factor the same negative yields a range of prints, and the negative's own tones stay exactly as they were exposed and can be printed again later.

questions.explanation: The negative is fixed once; printing time and paper contrast decide how the tones land. Longer printing darkens the sheet and shorter printing lightens it, so one negative can yield many densities.
questions.hint: The print's darkness is set at printing time.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why screen printing suits posters with a few bold colours.
questions.stem: A board note asks why screen printing suits a poster needing a small number of bold colours on a large sheet.

answer.exemplar: Screen printing makes each colour a separate stencil, so the number of inks, not the size of the sheet, drives the cost of colour changes. With only a handful of flat colours, a few screens produce large areas of solid, even ink that cannot be achieved as flatly by most other printing methods. The ink can be built up by repeated pulls to reach the required density, and the final poster is durable enough for outdoor posting because the ink sits on the surface as a solid film.

questions.explanation: Cost in screen printing scales with the number of inks, not with sheet size, so a poster with a handful of flat colours needs only a few screens. Repeated pulls can build dense, solid ink that other methods struggle to match.
questions.hint: Screen cost follows the number of inks.

options.text: Glossy papers contain more silver, so they always hold a wider tonal range
options.misconception: believes gloss comes from more silver in the emulsion

options.text: Matte papers are printed from negatives while glossy ones are contact printed
options.misconception: confuses surface finish with printing method

options.text: Glossy papers reflect a stronger sheen and give a deeper apparent black than matte stock

questions.explanation: A glossy surface throws a strong specular reflection, so highlights appear brighter and blacks deeper than on matte stock, which scatters light diffusely. Silver content, printing method and detail are separate matters.
questions.hint: Gloss changes how the paper reflects light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Three-colour construction of a colour print
questions.learningObjective: Draw a sound conclusion from a set of dot area percentages.
questions.stem: A colour print checklist on the board records dot area percentages for one patch: magenta 42, yellow 11, cyan 26, black 8.

options.text: Yellow leads the patch, since it carries the smallest coverage in the list
options.misconception: reads the smallest coverage as the leading colour

options.text: Magenta leads the patch, and the black contributes depth to the colour
The four values cannot belong to a single colour patch
options.misconception: believes a colour patch cannot carry four inks

options.text: Black covers most of the patch, so the patch must read as neutral black
options.misconception: confuses an 8 percent black with total coverage

questions.explanation: Magenta at 42 percent leads the mixture, and the 8 percent black layer deepens it toward a neutral, richer dark. The smallest coverage does not lead a mixture, and 8 percent is nowhere near a dominant black.
questions.hint: The largest coverage leads the mix.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The planographic principle of lithography
questions.learningObjective: Explain why corrections are possible on an unfixed lithographic stone.
questions.stem: A board note asks why a lithographic artist can redraw on the same stone during the proofing stage.

answer.exemplar: Lithographic grease and the dampened stone are reversible while the stone is still in working state, so a drawn line can be taken back up with gum and spirit rather than cut away. If the image is wrong, the greasy crayon is wiped off, the stone re-gummed, and the drawing corrected, then inked again. Once the stone has been fully gummed, etched and printed, the image is fixed, so corrections are no longer possible except by grinding the surface away and starting again.

questions.explanation: Before the fixing stages grease and stone are reversible, so a wrong line can be wiped up with gum and spirit and the drawing corrected. Once gummed, etched and printed, the image is fixed.
questions.hint: Corrections are possible only before fixing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The layer logic of screen printing
questions.learningObjective: Compute the total cost of a screen-printing job.
questions.stem: A screen-printing estimate on the board prices 4 screens at 18 units each and 3 screens at 22 units each. What is the total cost in units?
questions.explanation: Four screens at 18 units cost 72, and three at 22 units cost 66, giving 72 plus 66, which is 138 units. The count of screens at each price must be kept separate before the two amounts are added.
questions.hint: Price each group, then add the totals.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal inversion on a photographic negative
questions.learningObjective: Explain the density readings taken from a negative sleeve.

stimulus.body: The sleeve note reads: negative 27, daylight scene, sky reading 2.1 density, subject's white collar reading 0.3, black hat 2.6, image printed twice on different paper grades.

questions.stem: Using the sleeve note, a transit planner explains the readings given for the collar and the hat.

options.text: Both readings are equal, because paper grade changes the density on the negative
options.misconception: believes paper grade alters the negative's own densities

options.text: The collar is the brightest part of the scene and so the densest on the negative
options.misconception: reverses which areas of the scene read dense

options.text: The collar is the brightest part of the scene and so the thinnest on the negative
The readings describe the two prints, so the negative itself carries no tonal record
options.misconception: confuses the print readings with the negative's readings

questions.explanation: More light falls on the white collar than on the black hat, so the collar exposes the film least and stays thin at 0.3, while the hat at 2.6 is the densest area. Paper grade affects the prints only.
questions.hint: Denser negative means less light fell there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirrored surface of a daguerreotype
questions.learningObjective: Trace the formation and reversal of a daguerreotype image.
questions.stem: A closing board test asks two things about a daguerreotype: first, how the image on the plate was formed; second, why its lettering appears reversed.

options.text: First, by engraving the design on metal; second, because the plate was turned over for printing
options.misconception: invents an engraving and a flipping step

options.text: First, by contact printing a paper negative; second, because the plate was polished in reverse
options.misconception: describes contact printing and hand polishing

options.text: First, by coating glass with collodion; second, because the developer was applied the wrong way
options.misconception: confuses the collodion plate with the daguerreotype

options.text: First, by exposing a light-sensitive silvered plate; second, because a lens reverses the image

questions.explanation: A daguerreotype forms by exposing a polished, silvered plate carrying light-sensitive salts, and the image stays on that plate. Lettering reads backwards because the lens projects a reversed image and nothing turns it round.
questions.hint: The lens explains the reversal.
